title: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code
authors: Mark Chen, Jerry Tworek, Heewoo Jun, et al. (58 authors)
central_claim: Defines the unbiased pass@k estimator 1 - C(n-c,k)/C(n,k) from n >= k samples with c correct, and shows the plug-in 1-(1-p_hat)^k estimator is biased.
cite_claim: pass@k should be estimated with the unbiased estimator E[1 - C(n-c,k)/C(n,k)] using n >= k samples per task; the plug-in 1-(1-p_hat)^k consistently underestimates.
location: Sec. 2.1 'Functional Correctness', Eq. (1) and Fig. 3 (numerically stable numpy code); Appendix A 'Estimating pass@k', Fig. 13
quote: to evaluate pass@k, we generate n ≥ k samples per task (in this paper, we use n = 200 and k ≤ 100)
relevance: Origin of the combinatorial estimator that the pass^k estimator mirrors. Justifies computing pass^k per task from n >= k trials rather than p_hat^k; also shows why n = k (fiks: n = k = 5) is the minimum, not a good choice (per-task estimate collapses to an indicator).

title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
authors: Shunyu Yao, Noah Shinn, Pedram Razavi, Karthik Narasimhan
central_claim: Introduces pass^k, the probability that all k i.i.d. trials of a task succeed, averaged over tasks, estimated without bias as E_task[C(c,k)/C(n,k)].
cite_claim: pass^k = E_task[C(c,k)/C(n,k)] for a task run n times with c successes; it is the reliability analogue of Chen et al.'s pass@k.
quote: defined as the chance that all k i.i.d. task trials are successful, averaged across tasks
relevance: Reused key (benchmarks area). The estimator fiks reports for k = 1..5. Note it gives point estimates only; CIs must come from task-level resampling or a hierarchical model.

title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
authors: Evan Miller
central_claim: Treat evals as experiments: report CLT standard errors, cluster them when questions come in groups, reduce within-question variance by resampling, use paired differences between models, and run power analysis.
cite_claim: Clustered standard errors can be about 3x the naive SE when questions are grouped; paired SEs should be used for model comparisons wherever practicable; repeated samples of the same question are not independent and must be clustered.
location: Sec. 2.2 'Clustered questions' (Table 4: ratio 3.05 for DROP); Sec. 3.1 'Resampling'; Sec. 3.3 'Don't touch the thermostat!'; Sec. 4.2 'Paired analysis'; Sec. 5 'Power analysis' (Eq. 9-10)
quote: We therefore recommend using the paired version of the standard error estimate wherever practicable.
relevance: Primary methodological anchor for the analysis plan: trials nested in tasks are clustered data; with/without-fiks comparisons are paired by task; power formula n = (z_a/2+z_b)^2(omega^2 + sigma_A^2/K_A + sigma_B^2/K_B)/delta^2 gives the minimum detectable effect at fixed n.

title: Position: Don't Use the CLT in LLM Evals With Fewer Than a Few Hundred Datapoints
authors: Sam Bowyer, Laurence Aitchison, Desi R. Ivanova
venue_or_publisher: ICML 2025 (position paper, spotlight per authors' repo); arXiv:2503.01747
central_claim: CLT-based intervals (including clustered CLT) under-cover badly for small evals (N = 3-100); Wilson score or Beta-Binomial Bayesian intervals should be used, paired Bayesian comparisons for paired data, and bootstrap CIs also under-cover.
cite_claim: For small N, CLT and bootstrap intervals are too narrow; use Wilson or Bayesian intervals for single rates and a paired Bayesian method for paired model comparisons; only a clustered Bayesian model reached nominal coverage for clustered data.
location: Abstract; Sec. 3.1 (IID); Sec. 3.2 / Fig. 3 caption (clustered); Sec. 3.4 (paired); Sec. 3.5 (F1, bootstrap); Sec. 4 (no hard N threshold)
quote: We would, therefore, recommend using WS or Bayesian intervals in practice.
relevance: Directly governs fiks's regime (6 tasks x 5 trials; per-drift n = 5). Rules out naive CLT and percentile bootstrap as the primary interval at this scale; supports Wilson for rates and a hierarchical Bayesian model for clustered trials.

title: sambowyer/bayes_evals: a lightweight library for Bayesian analysis of LLM evals
authors: Sam Bowyer et al.
central_claim: Python implementation of the Bayesian intervals and independent/paired model comparisons recommended by Bowyer et al. 2025.
cite_claim: Provides independent_intervals, independent_comparisons and paired_comparisons for binary eval outcomes (MIT license).
quote: A lightweight library for Bayesian analysis of LLM evals (ICML 2025 Spotlight Position Paper)
relevance: Runnable sensitivity analysis for paper/scripts: paired Bayesian comparison of with-vs-without receipts. Does not implement the clustered model; fiks must add a task-level random effect itself.

title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks
authors: Yuxuan Zhu, Tengjun Jin, Yada Pruksachatkun, ..., Percy Liang, Daniel Kang
central_claim: Agentic Benchmark Checklist (ABC): task validity (T.1-T.10), outcome validity (O.a-O.i), and reporting (R.1-R.13); flaws such as tau-bench crediting a do-nothing agent on impossible tasks can mis-estimate performance by up to 100% relative.
cite_claim: Agentic benchmarks should verify ground truth and task solvability, check state-based outcomes for both relevant and irrelevant state, compare against trivial agents, and report measures of statistical significance.
location: Abstract; Sec. 1 (tau-bench trivial agent, 38%); Sec. 4.1 (T.7-T.10); Sec. 4.2 (O.g.1-O.g.3); Sec. 4.3 (R.10-R.13)
quote: a trivial agent that returns empty responses is considered successful on intentionally impossible tasks
relevance: Reused key (benchmarks area). A reviewer will apply ABC to fiks's grader: the D3 order task where 'could not confirm' is arguably correct is exactly the impossible-task issue; ABC R.12-R.13 asks for a trivial-agent baseline (always-decline).

title: Holistic Agent Leaderboard: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agent Evaluation
authors: Sayash Kapoor, Benedikt Stroebl, Peter Kirgis, Nitya Nadgir, Zachary S. Siegel, Boyi Wei, ..., Arvind Narayanan (31 authors)
central_claim: A standardized parallel harness ran 21,730 rollouts across 9 models and 9 benchmarks (~$40,000), reports accuracy-vs-cost Pareto frontiers in dollars and tokens, and uses LLM-assisted log inspection to surface shortcuts and unsafe actions.
cite_claim: Agent evaluations should report cost (dollars and tokens) alongside accuracy as a Pareto frontier and should include systematic log analysis, which surfaced benchmark-answer lookups and unsafe actions.
location: Abstract; cost reporting and log-inspection findings sections (HTML body; appendices not fully read)
quote: We validate the harness by conducting 21,730 agent rollouts across 9 models and 9 benchmarks
relevance: Justifies cost-per-PR and tokens-per-call columns and a log-inspection pass over fiks bench transcripts (fiks already did one for receipt wording). We did not find an explicit repeated-runs/CI recommendation in the part read [verify appendices].

title: AI Agents That Matter
authors: Sayash Kapoor, Benedikt Stroebl, Zachary S. Siegel, Nitya Nadgir, Arvind Narayanan
central_claim: Accuracy-only agent benchmarking yields needlessly costly agents; cost and accuracy should be jointly optimized; many agent benchmarks lack adequate holdout sets; inconsistent evaluation causes poor reproducibility.
cite_claim: Agent evaluations should jointly report cost and accuracy, and benchmarks need held-out sets to prevent overfitting.
quote: many agent benchmarks have inadequate holdout sets, and sometimes none at all.
relevance: Supports the blind-authored held-out drift suite (G3) as a holdout in the sense of this paper, and cost reporting for the repair agent.

title: Non-Determinism of "Deterministic" LLM Settings
authors: Berk Atil, Sarp Aykent, Alexa Chittams, Lisheng Fu, Rebecca J. Passonneau, et al.
central_claim: Five LLMs run 10 times on eight tasks under settings expected to be deterministic gave non-repeatable accuracy (up to 15% variation) and non-identical outputs.
cite_claim: LLM outputs under nominally deterministic settings vary across runs, with accuracy variation up to 15%, so single-run results are not reproducible.
quote: We see accuracy variations up to 15% across naturally occurring runs
relevance: Justifies k > 1 trials and per-trial logging even if fiks pinned temperature; supports reporting run-to-run variance per task.

title: Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference
authors: Horace He (Thinking Machines Lab)
central_claim: The main cause of inference nondeterminism for a user is lack of batch invariance: server load changes batch size, which changes kernel numerics.
cite_claim: Hosted LLM APIs are nondeterministic even at fixed sampling settings because kernels are not batch-invariant and batch size varies with server load.
location: Sections 'Batch invariance and "determinism"' and 'How do we make kernels batch-invariant?'
quote: the load (and thus batch-size) nondeterministically varies!
relevance: Mechanistic explanation for why fiks's hosted-model trials cannot be made deterministic by the client; seeds alone do not control variance. Industry blog, not peer reviewed.

title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to Testing Statistical Significance in Natural Language Processing
authors: Rotem Dror, Gili Baumer, Segev Shlomov, Roi Reichart
central_claim: Significance testing is often ignored or misused in ACL/TACL 2017 papers; proposes a protocol for choosing a test by task, setup and metric.
cite_claim: A survey of ACL and TACL 2017 papers found significance testing often ignored or misused; the authors give a protocol for test selection.
quote: a simple practical protocol for statistical significance test selection in NLP setups
relevance: Venue-norm citation for why every with-vs-without comparison carries a named test chosen in advance.

title: Statistical Significance Tests for Machine Translation Evaluation
authors: Philipp Koehn
central_claim: Introduces bootstrap CIs and paired bootstrap resampling for comparing two systems on the same test set; on BLEU the 95% bootstrap interval covered the near-true score in 97 of 100 test sets.
cite_claim: Paired bootstrap resampling over the same test items estimates the reliability of a 'system A beats B' conclusion.
quote: Loosely speaking, the 95% confidence level is actually 97% correct.
relevance: Origin of the paired bootstrap used for H3 (judge vs contracts AUROC). Coverage held at 300 items per set; Bowyer et al. show it fails at very small N, so for fiks it is secondary, resampling tasks (clusters), not calls.

title: A Hitchhiker's guide to statistical tests for assessing randomized algorithms in software engineering
authors: Andrea Arcuri, Lionel Briand
venue_or_publisher: Software Testing, Verification and Reliability 24(3):219-250 (extends ICSE 2011)
central_claim: Systematic review shows SE studies of randomized algorithms rarely account for randomness; gives guidelines: Fisher exact test for pass/fail outcomes, Vargha-Delaney A12 / odds ratio effect sizes, many runs, and report raw p-values rather than rely on Bonferroni.
cite_claim: For binary pass/fail outcomes use an exact test of proportions and report effect sizes; always report raw p-values, since Bonferroni-type adjustments have been widely criticized.
location: Sec. 4 'Statistical Difference' (Fisher exact); Sec. 7 'Effect Size' (A12, odds ratio); Sec. 8 'Number of Runs'; Sec. 9 'Multiple Tests'
quote: it is important to always report the obtained p-values, not just whether a difference is significant
relevance: The SE-venue standard (ICSE/TSE reviewers cite it). The repair agent and bench agent are randomized algorithms in its sense. It tempers ORCHESTRATION's mandatory correction: correct a pre-registered confirmatory family (Holm) but also report raw p-values and effect sizes.

title: Approximate Statistical Tests for Comparing Supervised Classification Learning Algorithms
authors: Thomas G. Dietterich
central_claim: Among five tests, the difference-of-proportions test and resampled paired t test have high type I error; McNemar's test has low type I error and is the only acceptable test when an algorithm can be run once.
cite_claim: When two classifiers (detectors) are evaluated once on the same items, McNemar's test on discordant items is the test with acceptable type I error; the unpaired difference-of-proportions test should not be used.
quote: For algorithms that can be executed only once, Mc-Nemar's test is the only test with acceptable type I error.
relevance: Justifies McNemar on discordant calls for fiks contracts vs schema-only / LLM-judge detectors on the same labeled calls (H1, H3), instead of comparing two marginal detection rates.

title: Note on the Sampling Error of the Difference Between Correlated Proportions or Percentages
authors: Quinn McNemar
central_claim: Original test for the difference between two correlated (paired) proportions, based on discordant pairs.
cite_claim: The difference between two proportions measured on the same units must be tested with a paired (correlated-proportions) test.
quote: Two formulas are presented for judging the significance of the difference between correlated proportions.
relevance: Primary reference for the paired detector and paired with/without-receipt comparisons.

title: The McNemar test for binary matched-pairs data: mid-p and asymptotic are better than exact conditional
authors: Morten W. Fagerland, Stian Lydersen, Petter Laake
central_claim: The exact conditional McNemar test is very conservative (type I error often half the nominal level or less); the mid-p version and even the asymptotic test perform well at small sample sizes.
cite_claim: For small matched-pairs samples, prefer the McNemar mid-p test over the exact conditional test, which is overly conservative.
quote: The easy-to-calculate mid-p test is an excellent alternative to the complex exact unconditional test.
relevance: Choose mid-p McNemar in the pre-registration. Illustrative arithmetic (ours): with all discordant pairs favoring one arm, exact needs 6 discordant units for p < .05, mid-p needs 5; with 6 tasks and at most 2 discordant tasks (pass^5 3/6 vs 5/6), no task-level test can reach significance.

title: Probable Inference, the Law of Succession, and Statistical Inference
authors: Edwin B. Wilson
venue_or_publisher: Journal of the American Statistical Association 22(158):209-212
central_claim: Introduces the score interval for a binomial proportion (Wilson interval).
cite_claim: The Wilson score interval for a binomial proportion was introduced by Wilson (1927).
location: Whole article (Crossref metadata confirmed; full text not read)
quote: Probable Inference, the Law of Succession, and Statistical Inference
relevance: Citation for every rate CI in the paper (detection, FP, pass^1).

title: Interval Estimation for a Binomial Proportion
authors: Lawrence D. Brown, T. Tony Cai, Anirban DasGupta
central_claim: The Wald interval's coverage is erratic even at moderate n; recommends Wilson or equal-tailed Jeffreys for small n and Agresti-Coull for larger n.
cite_claim: For small n, use the Wilson or Jeffreys interval for a binomial proportion, not the Wald interval.
quote: we recommend the Wilson interval or the equal-tailed Jeffreys prior interval for small n
relevance: Justifies Wilson (with Jeffreys as sensitivity) for every per-drift rate at n = 5-30.

title: If nothing goes wrong, is everything all right? Interpreting zero numerators
authors: James A. Hanley, Abby Lippman-Hand
central_claim: With zero events in n trials, an approximate 95% upper confidence bound on the event rate is 3/n (rule of three).
cite_claim: Zero observed false positives in n clean results bounds the FP rate only at about 3/n (95%).
location: Whole article (Crossref metadata confirmed; rule as stated in Wikipedia 'Rule of three (statistics)', which cites this article). Full text not read [verify wording].
quote: If nothing goes wrong, is everything all right?
relevance: fiks's '0 violated receipts in 30 v1 trials' bounds the per-trial FP rate only at ~10% (Wilson 11.3%). H5's Wilson upper bound <= 2% needs >= 189 clean receipts with 0 FPs (280 with 1 FP), computed here.

title: A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure
authors: Sture Holm
central_claim: Step-down procedure that controls the family-wise error rate and is uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni.
cite_claim: Holm's step-down procedure controls the family-wise error rate with uniformly more power than Bonferroni.
location: Citation and description from the Wikipedia article 'Holm-Bonferroni method' (original not opened) [verify against JSTOR 4615733]
quote: intended to control the family-wise error rate
relevance: The correction ORCHESTRATION names; applied to the confirmatory family of primary endpoints only.

title: Comparing the Areas under Two or More Correlated Receiver Operating Characteristic Curves: A Nonparametric Approach
authors: Elizabeth R. DeLong, David M. DeLong, Daniel L. Clarke-Pearson
central_claim: Nonparametric (U-statistic) test for the difference between AUCs of two or more correlated ROC curves measured on the same cases.
cite_claim: AUROCs of two detectors scored on the same items should be compared with a paired test such as DeLong's nonparametric method.
location: Whole article (Crossref metadata confirmed; full text not read)
quote: Comparing the Areas under Two or More Correlated Receiver Operating Characteristic Curves: A Nonparametric Approach
relevance: Applies to H3 (LLM judge vs contracts). Caveat: DeLong assumes independent cases; fiks calls are clustered in trials and tasks, so a task-level cluster bootstrap is the primary and DeLong a secondary. Binary contracts have a one-point ROC, so AUROC equals balanced accuracy for them.

title: Fast Implementation of DeLong's Algorithm for Comparing the Areas Under Correlated Receiver Operating Characteristic Curves
authors: Xu Sun, Weichao Xu
central_claim: O(n log n) implementation of DeLong's covariance estimator.
cite_claim: DeLong's test can be computed efficiently with the Sun-Xu algorithm.
location: Whole article (Crossref metadata confirmed; not read)
quote: Fast Implementation of DeLong's Algorithm
relevance: Implementation reference if we write DeLong in Python instead of calling pROC.

title: pROC: Display and Analyze ROC Curves (R package)
authors: Xavier Robin et al.
venue_or_publisher: CRAN (GPL >= 3); Robin et al., BMC Bioinformatics 2011
central_claim: R package that compares (partial) AUCs with U-statistic (DeLong) or bootstrap tests.
cite_claim: pROC compares AUCs with U-statistic or bootstrap tests.
quote: (Partial) area under the curve (AUC) can be compared with statistical tests based on U-statistics or bootstrap.
relevance: Reference implementation to cross-check our Python DeLong/bootstrap numbers in paper/scripts (run as an external tool; GPL does not touch fiks code).

title: statsmodels: proportion_confint and contingency_tables.mcnemar
authors: statsmodels developers
central_claim: proportion_confint supports normal, agresti_coull, beta (Clopper-Pearson), wilson, jeffreys and binom_test intervals; mcnemar supports exact (binomial) and chi-square with continuity correction, with no documented mid-p option.
cite_claim: statsmodels provides Wilson, Jeffreys and Clopper-Pearson intervals and an exact/asymptotic McNemar test.
quote: wilson : Wilson Score interval
relevance: Implementation for paper/scripts. Mid-p McNemar must be computed by hand (exact p minus half the point probability).

title: Sample Size for Testing Differences in Proportions for the Paired-Sample Design
authors: Roger J. Connor
central_claim: Sample-size formula for McNemar-type paired-proportion comparisons as a function of the discordant-cell probabilities.
cite_claim: Power for paired proportions depends on the discordant probabilities p10 and p01, not on the marginal rates alone.
location: Whole article (Crossref metadata confirmed; full text not read) [verify formula]
quote: Sample Size for Testing Differences in Proportions for the Paired-Sample Design
relevance: Power analysis for H1/H3/H12. Illustrative (ours, using the formula usually attributed to Connor, [verify]): p10 = .30, p01 = .05 needs about 42 paired units at alpha .05, power .8; p10 = .20, p01 = .05 needs about 85.

title: Bootstrapping Clustered Data
authors: Christopher A. Field, Alan H. Welsh
venue_or_publisher: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B 69(3):369-390
central_claim: Analyses which bootstraps for one-way clustered data (resample clusters, resample within, both) are consistent under which models; theory is mixed and model-dependent.
cite_claim: How clustered data are bootstrapped (clusters vs within-cluster units) determines validity; the theory for nonparametric cluster bootstraps is limited and mixed.
quote: Various bootstraps have been proposed for bootstrapping clustered data from one-way arrays.
relevance: Justifies resampling tasks (clusters) with trials kept intact, and caution in calling a cluster bootstrap over 6 clusters valid.

title: Are mutants a valid substitute for real faults in software testing?
authors: René Just, Darioush Jalali, Laura Inozemtseva, Michael D. Ernst, Reid Holmes, Gordon Fraser
central_claim: On 357 real faults in 5 Java programs, 73% are coupled to mutants from common operators; mutant detection correlates with real-fault detection independently of coverage; 17% (algorithm changes, code deletion, invariant violations, numerical errors) are not coupled to any mutant.
cite_claim: Mutant detection is significantly correlated with real fault detection independently of coverage, and 73% of real faults are coupled to mutants; but 27% are not coupled to common-operator mutants, including faults from violated pre/post-conditions or invariants.
location: Sec. 1 contributions; Sec. 3.1; Sec. 3.2 'What Types of Real Faults Are Not Coupled to Mutants?' (Table 4); Sec. 3.3 (Fig. 8)
quote: 27% of real faults are not coupled to the mutants generated by commonly used mutation operators.
relevance: Core argument for M2: seeded faults are acceptable evidence when (a) they are generated by a predeclared operator set and (b) coupling to real faults is checked. fiks should test coupling between its drift operators and the real-bug set R1-R25. Also a warning: the faults fiks targets (semantic/invariant) are the kind that mutation operators couple to least.

title: Are Mutation Scores Correlated with Real Fault Detection? A Large Scale Empirical Study on the Relationship Between Mutants and Real Faults
authors: Mike Papadakis, Donghwan Shin, Shin Yoo, Doo-Hwan Bae
central_claim: [verify] Reports that the correlation between mutation score and real-fault detection is weak once test-suite size is controlled for.
cite_claim: [verify] Mutation score alone is a weak predictor of real-fault detection after controlling for test-suite size.
location: Whole article (Crossref/Semantic Scholar metadata confirmed; full text 403, not read)
quote: Are Mutation Scores Correlated with Real Fault Detection?
relevance: Strongest critique of the mutants-as-proxy argument; if verified, it says fiks must not rest representativeness on mutation analysis alone and needs the real-bug harness.

title: Is mutation an appropriate tool for testing experiments?
authors: James H. Andrews, Lionel C. Briand, Yvan Labiche
central_claim: [verify] Generated mutants behave like real faults in detection difficulty, whereas hand-seeded faults are harder to detect than real faults and give a biased view.
cite_claim: [verify] Hand-seeded faults may not represent real faults; mechanically generated mutants were closer to real faults in the subject programs.
location: Whole article (Crossref metadata confirmed; closed access, not read)
quote: Is mutation an appropriate tool for testing experiments?
relevance: The canonical source for reviewer objection M2 (author hand-seeded faults are biased). Supports generating drifts from a predeclared operator set by someone other than the contract author.

title: Mutations: How Close are they to Real Faults?
authors: Rahul Gopinath, Carlos Jensen, Alex Groce
central_claim: [verify] Compares real bug-fix changes mined from repositories with typical mutation operators, finding real fixes often differ from single-operator mutations.
cite_claim: [verify] Real faults mined from fix histories differ in size and kind from standard mutation operators.
location: Whole article (Crossref metadata confirmed; not read)
quote: Mutations: How Close are they to Real Faults?
relevance: Supports deriving drift operators from mined real API/MCP fixes (fiks's real-bugs areas) rather than from generic code mutations.

title: Test oracle assessment and improvement
authors: Gunel Jahangirova, David Clark, Mark Harman, Paolo Tonella
central_claim: Assesses assertion oracles by false positives (generated tests revealing assertions that fail on correct behaviour) and false negatives (mutants that pass the assertion); improvement raised oracle fault detection by 48.6% on average.
cite_claim: An oracle's quality is measured by both false positives on correct executions and false negatives on mutated (faulty) executions; test generation finds the first and mutation testing finds the second.
quote: Our technique combines test case generation to reveal false positives and mutation testing to reveal false negatives.
relevance: fiks contracts are runtime oracles. This gives the principled adequacy protocol: FP on benign/v1/v1b traffic (generated benign evolutions) plus FN on response-level mutants of recorded upstream payloads.

title: Service-Level Fault Injection Testing
authors: Christopher S. Meiklejohn, Andrea Estrada, Yiwen Song, Heather Miller, Rohan Padhye
central_claim: Filibuster extends functional tests to inject service-call faults (call-site exceptions and HTTP error responses); evaluated on a corpus of 8 small and 4 industrial microservice apps whose bugs were reconstructed from a systematic review of 50 public chaos-engineering presentations (32 companies).
cite_claim: Because real microservice bugs are rarely public, Filibuster built its benchmark by systematically reviewing 50 industry chaos-engineering talks and re-implementing the bugs; its fault model covers exceptions and error responses and explicitly does not consider corrupted responses.
location: Abstract; Sec. 2 (corpus construction, 50 presentations / 32 companies); Sec. 5 fault list ('Callsite exceptions', 'Error responses'); Sec. 8 'Discussion: Limitations and Future Work' (Nondeterminism)
quote: our design does not consider the corruption of service responses
relevance: Two uses: (1) precedent for a principled author-built fault corpus derived from a systematic review of public incident reports (fiks's S1-S12 from mined MCP/API issues follows the same recipe); (2) the closest dependency-fault-injection tool explicitly excludes the wrong-but-successful responses fiks targets. Repo: Apache-2.0 (github.com/filibuster-testing/filibuster).

title: Lineage-driven Fault Injection
authors: Peter Alvaro, Joshua Rosen, Joseph M. Hellerstein
central_claim: Reasons backwards from correct outcomes (data lineage) plus SAT solving to find fault combinations that could prevent them; Molly finds bugs with an order of magnitude fewer executions than random injection or certifies the configuration bug-free.
cite_claim: Fault injection can be targeted by reasoning backwards from the lineage of a correct outcome to faults that could prevent it, instead of random injection.
quote: A lineage-driven fault injector reasons backwards from correct system outcomes to determine whether failures in the execution could have prevented the outcome.
relevance: Methodological analogue for read-after-write postconditions and for choosing which upstream fields to perturb (those the agent's answer depends on). Fault model is omission/crash, not value corruption.

title: Chaos Engineering
authors: Ali Basiri, Niosha Behnam, Ruud de Rooij, Lorin Hochstein, Luke Kosewski, Justin Reynolds, Casey Rosenthal
central_claim: Netflix's principles: hypothesize about steady state, vary real-world events, run experiments in production, automate continuously; choose fault stimuli from historical outage data.
cite_claim: Injected faults should be sampled from real-world events, using historical outage data where available.
quote: One obvious choice is to look at historical data to see what type of inputs were involved in previous system outages
relevance: Industry argument for when injected faults are representative: drawn from incident history. fiks's drift classes trace to mined issues (C3, real-bug areas), which is this recipe.

title: Assessing Dependability with Software Fault Injection: A Survey
authors: Roberto Natella, Domenico Cotroneo, Henrique S. Madeira
central_claim: Survey of software fault injection, organized around fault representativeness, efficiency and usability.
cite_claim: Fault representativeness is a central, explicitly evaluated property of software fault injection approaches.
quote: discusses how these approaches have evolved to achieve fault representativeness, efficiency, and usability
relevance: Frames M2 in the dependability literature's own vocabulary: the paper should argue representativeness explicitly (provenance of each drift class, field-data frequency).

title: Emulation of Software Faults: A Field Data Study and a Practical Approach
authors: João A. Durães, Henrique S. Madeira
central_claim: [verify] Field study of real software faults in open-source programs used to derive a representative fault-type set and the G-SWFIT emulation technique.
cite_claim: [verify] Representative fault injection derives its fault types and their relative frequencies from field data on real faults.
location: Whole article (Crossref metadata confirmed; closed access, not read)
quote: Emulation of Software Faults: A Field Data Study and a Practical Approach
relevance: Recipe for weighting drift classes by observed frequency (e.g., C3's category shares) rather than equally, if the paper reports pooled detection rates.

title: WireMock documentation: Simulating Faults
authors: WireMock project
central_claim: WireMock simulates fixed/random/chunked-dribble delays and bad responses (EMPTY_RESPONSE, MALFORMED_RESPONSE_CHUNK, RANDOM_DATA_THEN_CLOSE, CONNECTION_RESET_BY_PEER).
cite_claim: Mainstream service-virtualization fault menus cover latency and transport/protocol corruption; semantic value drift must be hand-authored as stub bodies.
quote: the response will not be returned until after the specified number of milliseconds
relevance: Shows that standard fault-injection tooling does not model fiks's silent semantic drifts out of the box; usable as an independent substrate for the blind-authored drift suite (license Apache-2.0 [verify]).

title: Hoverfly documentation: Modes (Capture, Simulate, Spy, Synthesize, Modify, Diff)
authors: SpectoLabs / Hoverfly project
central_claim: Hoverfly's Diff mode forwards each request to the real service and compares the real response with the stored simulation; Modify mode passes requests and responses through middleware.
cite_claim: Service virtualization tools can diff live responses against recorded ones (Diff mode) and rewrite traffic through middleware (Modify mode).
quote: In this mode, Hoverfly forwards a request to an external service and compares a response with currently stored simulation.
relevance: A runnable 'recorded-response oracle' baseline for RQ1 (flags any deviation from v1 recordings: high recall on drift, but every benign change is a false positive). Modify mode is a ready drift injector for third-party substrates. License Apache-2.0 [verify].

title: Shopify/toxiproxy
authors: Shopify
central_claim: TCP proxy for simulating network conditions with toxics: latency, down, bandwidth, slow_close, timeout, reset_peer, slicer, limit_data, packet_loss.
cite_claim: Toxiproxy's built-in toxics act on the transport pipe (delay, throttle, slice, drop, close), not on payload semantics.
quote: Toxics manipulate the pipe between the client and upstream.
relevance: Negative-control substrate: transport faults surface as errors, which fiks is not designed for; shows the gap between chaos tooling and silent semantic drift.
